dataset.title: De-identified dementia-care workflow knowledge — AI apprentice training set
dataset.scope: Psychologist-led, non-pharmacological management of mid- to late-stage dementia in specialist nursing homes

readme.Purpose: De-identified, time-ordered extraction of clinical/workflow knowledge from 14 recorded conversations (Jun–Sep 2026) about how a specialist operator and its psychologists care for and manage residents with mid- to late-stage dementia using a CBT-informed, non-pharmacological method. Intended as training data for an AI apprentice.
readme.What was kept: Only content relevant to care workflow and clinical knowledge: goals of care, non-drug interventions, refusal and behaviour management, assessment and care planning, roles and coordination, documentation practices, training/supervision, measurement, implementation fidelity, and interviewer elicitation technique.
readme.What was removed: All commercial and confidential business content (licensing, pilot and term-sheet terms, valuations, exits, revenue, costs, investor/board matters, market sizing), personal small talk, health/bereavement disclosures, travel, political opinions, named third parties, and identifying operational statistics. See 'excluded_content_categories' per session.
readme.De-identification: Names of people, companies, brands, software vendors and locations replaced with bracketed placeholders (see Deid_Legend). No mapping to real identities is included. Long or mixed interviewer turns were paraphrased (text_type = 'paraphrased') to strip business content; all other dialogue is verbatim after placeholder substitution.
readme.Timestamps: start/end are offsets (HH:MM:SS) from the start of each recording, taken directly from the source VTT cues. session_date is the call date (2026). sort_key = date + offset, giving a single chronological ordering across all sessions. Wall-clock times are not available in the sources.
readme.Sheets: Sessions → session index & exclusion log; Timeline → condensed chronological view of every knowledge unit; Knowledge_Units → full learning records (question, why it was asked, expert answer, clinical rationale, key points, practice rules, cautions); Dialogue → de-identified relevant turns with English translations of French; Glossary; Deid_Legend.
readme.How to read a knowledge unit: interviewer_question = what was asked; question_intent_why = why the interviewer asked it; expert_answer = what the expert said; clinical_rationale_why = the underlying reason; practice_rules = actionable heuristics; cautions_or_corrections = misconceptions corrected or claims to treat carefully; source_type distinguishes expert statements from interviewer hypotheses.
readme.Reliability notes: Interviewer hypotheses/analyses (e.g., coding-error percentages from a small sample) are flagged and should not be treated as clinical facts. Numerical figures quoted by experts (e.g., ~50% of behaviours with somatic triggers) are recollections, not cited studies. S13 French turns were translated for this dataset; original French is retained alongside.
readme.Empty recordings: S06 (2026-07-17) and S08 (2026-07-27 part 2) contain a single fragment each and yield no content; kept in the index for completeness.

knowledge_units.subtopic: Is progress under a non-drug approach measurable?
knowledge_units.interviewer_question: How can the effect of a non-drug, CBT-informed dementia care method be demonstrated with measurable indicators (compared with 'proving yoga works')?
knowledge_units.question_intent_why: She needs objective indicators that an outside organisation could agree on, so that adoption of the method can be judged on evidence rather than narrative.
knowledge_units.expert_answer: Unlike a lifestyle practice, the method rests on a scientific base (CBT principles). Progress is measurable with standardised instruments — e.g., the MMSE for cognition and the NPI for behavioural problems — but only if they are administered on a regular, repeated basis.
knowledge_units.clinical_rationale_why: A single assessment says little in a progressive disease; repeated measurement over time is what makes trajectories interpretable.
key_points: Method is grounded in CBT principles adapted to dementia.
Standardised instruments exist: MMSE (cognition), NPI (neuropsychiatric/behavioural symptoms).
Measurement must be regular to be meaningful.
practice_rules: Schedule standardised assessments at fixed intervals rather than ad hoc.
Interpret any single score against the resident's own previous scores.

knowledge_units.subtopic: Dose and fidelity: why partial adoption gives diluted results
knowledge_units.interviewer_question: (Context) If the method is packaged into software/training for other facilities, what results should be expected?
knowledge_units.question_intent_why: She is trying to understand how much of the outcome depends on full immersion versus transferable components, to set realistic targets.
knowledge_units.expert_answer: The effects the operator observes come from applying 100% of the method, with 100% of staff trained, 100% of the day. Other facilities using only parts (e.g., via online training or software) will apply a highly diluted version, so outcomes cannot be the same; targets must be set relative to each site's own baseline.
knowledge_units.clinical_rationale_why: The approach is a continuous way of interacting with residents; its effect is cumulative and depends on consistency across all staff and all moments of the day.
key_points: Full effect requires whole-team training and application throughout the day.
Partial uptake ⇒ diluted, smaller effects.
Benchmarks must be relative to a site's own baseline, not to the originating homes.
practice_rules: Do not promise the originating homes' results to a site adopting only components.
Assess the degree of adoption (who is trained, how much of the day) before judging effectiveness.

knowledge_units.subtopic: Choosing indicators that can move within 3–6 months
knowledge_units.interviewer_question: Out of the existing data catalogue (refusal, diet/hydration, sleep, activity engagement), which indicator best shows day-to-day progress within 3–6 months?
knowledge_units.question_intent_why: Big outcomes (dependency score, slower decline) are too slow and too broad for a short evaluation window; she wants an intermediate 'daily calories'-type indicator.
knowledge_units.expert_answer: The expert agreed to look for a candidate but stressed a precondition: such indicators only work if staff actually measure and record them. You cannot just 'witness' progress — and much of this information is currently not entered in the care software.
knowledge_units.clinical_rationale_why: Process indicators are only as good as the completeness of frontline documentation; absent data looks like absent change.
key_points: Global outcomes (dependency, 'slower decline') are not demonstrable within 6 months.
Candidate short-horizon indicators: refusal rate/type, diet & hydration, sleep, activity engagement.
Data completeness is the main constraint — many observations are never entered.
practice_rules: Before choosing an indicator, verify it is already being recorded consistently.
Prefer indicators tied to routine documentation over ones requiring new data collection.
knowledge_units.cautions_or_corrections: The 'weight-loss camp' analogies are the interviewer's framing, not clinical guidance.

knowledge_units.subtopic: Limits of a pharmacological cure
knowledge_units.interviewer_question: (Aside) If one day a weekly pill made dementia disappear…
knowledge_units.question_intent_why: Rhetorical framing of the market; not a clinical question.
knowledge_units.expert_answer: The expert noted that even a curative drug would not solve loneliness/solitude — the social dimension of life in care remains.
knowledge_units.clinical_rationale_why: Non-drug care addresses psychosocial needs (connection, meaning, pleasure) that medication does not.
key_points: Social isolation is a care target in its own right, independent of disease-modifying treatment.

knowledge_units.subtopic: Operational analytics vs method-level indicators
knowledge_units.interviewer_question: Can we layer activity engagement onto resident records and agree on progress indicators beyond the operational reports produced by the care software?
knowledge_units.question_intent_why: She distinguishes facility-management analytics from indicators that reflect the care method itself.
knowledge_units.expert_answer: (Interviewer statement) Existing software reports show operational views — e.g., nursing hours by activity type and which residents consume the most dependency hours — useful for resource allocation but not for judging the method. Refusal reduction and activity-engagement rate were flagged as the most meaningful method-level indicators.
knowledge_units.clinical_rationale_why: Resource-use metrics describe workload, not whether the care approach is working for the resident.
key_points: Operational analytics: hours by activity type; dependency hours per resident.
Method-level candidates: refusal reduction; activity-engagement rate.

knowledge_units.subtopic: Ongoing process, not crisis response — pleasure as a natural antidepressant
knowledge_units.interviewer_question: (Reviewing draft wording about product outcomes) How should results of the method be described?
knowledge_units.question_intent_why: She was framing outcomes as action→result; the expert corrected the causal model.
knowledge_units.expert_answer: The method is not like injecting a drug during a crisis; it is an ongoing process (like healthy food and exercise). Example: pleasure is used as a natural antidepressant — antidepressant medication is not stopped overnight, but pleasurable moments are provided every day, ideally several times a day, so the person experiences a stable sense of pleasure, feels good about herself and rebuilds self-esteem. This shifts overall state of mind and even eating. Relevant metrics are therefore repetition of actions: how often residents engage in activities, amount of social interaction, participation in outings, and whether activities offered match the person's psychological profile.
knowledge_units.clinical_rationale_why: Mood and behaviour respond to sustained exposure to positive experiences and self-esteem, not to one-off interventions.
key_points: Effect = cumulative result of repeated actions over time.
Pleasure/positive experiences as a 'natural antidepressant'; any drug reduction is gradual.
Process metrics: frequency of engagement, social interaction, outings, match between activities and psychological profile.
practice_rules: Plan several pleasurable moments per day for low-mood residents.
Never describe the approach as a quick fix; measure exposure/frequency.
Match activities to the individual's psychological profile and history.
knowledge_units.cautions_or_corrections: Medication changes remain a medical decision; the expert described gradual reduction, not abrupt withdrawal.

knowledge_units.subtopic: How frontline staff actually record care
knowledge_units.interviewer_question: How does recording work on the front line — does every staff member have a tablet or notepad? How do they remember, and how does a supervisor know a task was done?
knowledge_units.question_intent_why: She needs the real data-generation process to know what the records mean and what is feasible to track.
knowledge_units.expert_answer: It varies by home: some nurses have laptops or tablets; care assistants (who do most hands-on work) have no portable device. Staff go into rooms with their training, equipment and knowledge of the care plan, then enter what they did at a fixed PC after a round (e.g., after helping 8 residents wash) or at the end of the shift — from memory, not in real time. There is no clock-in/out. Schedules allocate residents per carer; if a resident refuses in the morning, the task is retried later that morning or in the afternoon. Supervisors know through the later PC entries.
knowledge_units.clinical_rationale_why: Documentation timing and device access shape data quality; memory-based batch entry loses detail and timing.
key_points: Care assistants have no portable devices; nurses sometimes do.
Entries are batch, memory-based, after rounds or end of shift.
Refused tasks are rescheduled within the day.
practice_rules: Treat entry time as an upper bound, not the event time.
Design any recording aid for fixed PCs unless devices are available.

knowledge_units.subtopic: What the records contain: boxes, figures and narrative
knowledge_units.interviewer_question: Is the software just qualitative comments based on what staff remember?
knowledge_units.question_intent_why: She is mapping data types to potential indicators.
knowledge_units.expert_answer: It depends on the topic: binary tick boxes for tasks (medication given? taken? toileting done?), figures for things like weight monitoring, and qualitative notes for behaviour — e.g., a resident agitated and repeatedly asking when her daughter is coming because she knew a visit was due, which is very different from 'diaper changed at 11'.
knowledge_units.clinical_rationale_why: Behavioural events need narrative because their meaning lies in context, triggers and the person's emotional state.
key_points: Binary: medication given/taken, toileting.
Numeric: weight.
Narrative: behaviour, emotional state, context (e.g., anticipatory anxiety before a family visit).
practice_rules: When analysing behaviour, read the narrative, not just coded fields.

knowledge_units.subtopic: Discovery approach: start from job and task descriptions
knowledge_units.interviewer_question: Could we get an overview of all workflows frontline staff follow — job and task descriptions, like a day-zero guide?
knowledge_units.question_intent_why: Her goal is not to create new workflows but to use what is already recorded within existing workflows and structure it for refusal reduction.
knowledge_units.expert_answer: The expert agreed to provide job/task descriptions per staff category.
knowledge_units.clinical_rationale_why: Understanding scope of practice per role tells you which observations each role can and should document.
key_points: Map role-specific tasks before designing indicators.
Aim: track within existing workflows rather than adding new ones.

knowledge_units.subtopic: Why recording is incomplete — and which domains are complete
knowledge_units.interviewer_question: How does the head nurse know who performs well? If recording is mandatory, why isn't it always done?
knowledge_units.question_intent_why: She is probing incentives and causes of missing data.
knowledge_units.expert_answer: There are no formal performance metrics — basics like attendance, punctuality and completing tasks within the timeframe. Recording is obligatory but not always done: staff turnover, day-only temporary staff (new software access needed each time), and discipline. Everything strictly healthcare-related (injections, drugs, dressings) is recorded ~100%; social activities, behaviour changes and refusals are not systematically recorded, because the general operator's focus is healthcare, whereas these are the method's focus.
knowledge_units.clinical_rationale_why: What gets documented reflects institutional priorities; psychosocial care is under-documented where medical tasks are prioritised.
key_points: Medical tasks: near-complete documentation.
Refusals, behaviour, social activity: inconsistent.
Drivers: turnover, temporary staff, access friction, discipline, priorities.
practice_rules: Expect psychosocial data gaps; do not interpret missing entries as absence of events.

knowledge_units.subtopic: Consistency of records; MMSE and individual cognitive care plans
knowledge_units.interviewer_question: So documentation depends on the person?
knowledge_units.question_intent_why: She is assessing reliability across residents and homes.
knowledge_units.expert_answer: Information is very inconsistent across residents, teams and homes. Often the psychologist or activity staff fill in activity information, supervised only by one specialist spread across several homes. What is consistent is the MMSE. Individual cognitive care plans are not 100% complete — they are a lot of work (reviewing existing ones plus new admissions), are specific to this method, and staff must be pushed to do them; some homes are behind.
knowledge_units.clinical_rationale_why: Comprehensive individualised plans are labour-intensive; backlogs occur with admissions and reviews.
key_points: MMSE: consistently recorded.
Individual cognitive care plans: valuable but often incomplete/backlogged.
Activity information often entered by psychologist or activity staff.
practice_rules: Prioritise completing plans for new admissions and scheduled reviews.

knowledge_units.subtopic: When a resident deteriorates: whose responsibility?
knowledge_units.interviewer_question: If a resident's dependency score rises by >10%, who is responsible?
knowledge_units.question_intent_why: She is looking for KPI ownership and escalation triggers.
knowledge_units.expert_answer: It is no one's fault — the disease evolves. A marked change flags the case for a multidisciplinary staff meeting: is the person showing more behavioural problems, more depression, something else? The team studies the case, finds reasons and puts strategies in place to resolve the situation or slow the process. Staff meetings happen daily and discuss observed cases; they do not need numeric data — the operation is qualitative-observation driven, not data driven.
knowledge_units.clinical_rationale_why: Decline is expected in progressive dementia; the clinical question is what changed and why, not who failed.
key_points: Deterioration ⇒ multidisciplinary case review, not blame.
Daily staff meetings discuss observations.
Look for behavioural change, depression or other causes; aim to resolve or slow.
practice_rules: Use a non-blaming case review when a resident's status changes.
Ask first: behavioural change? mood? physical cause?
knowledge_units.cautions_or_corrections: Interviewer expected data-driven ownership; expert corrected that practice is observation-driven.

knowledge_units.subtopic: Example of rich qualitative notes
knowledge_units.interviewer_question: (Expert reads live from a resident record.)
knowledge_units.question_intent_why: Illustrates what information exists even when it is not numeric.
knowledge_units.expert_answer: Example notes: resident very agitated during nursing care, verbally aggressive, pushing her chair with her feet, trying to stand with high fall risk, crying constantly; medication given; sat in the living room. Another: since diet changed to a mixed/grated texture she eats on her own and seems to enjoy it. Another: distressed during washing, foot pain, oedema, not wearing compression stockings. The goal is not productivity counts ('8 washes in 30 minutes').
knowledge_units.clinical_rationale_why: These notes link behaviour to physical causes (pain, oedema) and to environmental adaptations (food texture) — the reasoning chain the method relies on.
key_points: Agitation, verbal aggression and fall risk can co-occur during personal care.
Diet texture adaptation can restore independent eating and enjoyment.
Pain/oedema during washing may underlie distress.
practice_rules: When distress occurs during personal care, check for pain and physical discomfort.
Consider texture-modified diets when eating difficulties appear.

knowledge_units.subtopic: Role clarity is high; measurement is qualitative
knowledge_units.interviewer_question: It seems KPI ownership is virtually non-existent?
knowledge_units.question_intent_why: She inferred a lack of structure from the lack of metrics.
knowledge_units.expert_answer: The expert disagreed: each personnel type has very specific tasks and scope — nurses know what they are allowed to do, as do assistant nurses and cleaning staff. What everyone has to do is clear; the measurement is qualitative, not data-driven.
knowledge_units.clinical_rationale_why: Absence of metrics does not imply absence of role structure.
key_points: Roles and scopes of practice are clearly defined.
Performance is judged qualitatively.

knowledge_units.subtopic: Escalation path for repeated refusal (e.g., >3 refusals/day of drinking or eating)
knowledge_units.interviewer_question: If a resident refuses the same thing (e.g., drinking or eating) more than three times a day, when does that trigger a care-plan review, and whose responsibility is it — psychologist or nurse?
knowledge_units.question_intent_why: She wants an explicit trigger and owner for escalation.
knowledge_units.expert_answer: If severe enough it is brought to the (daily) staff meeting. Responsibility is multidisciplinary: any situation is linked to a physical problem, a neuropsychological problem, or both. The team does a 360° inquiry to find the root cause. Physical → care staff act (e.g., change treatment via the doctor, new mattress). Psychological/behavioural without a physical cause → psychologist, possibly with activity staff, devises strategies. The cognitive care plan is revised only if the change is durable. Identification is collective; resolution is owned by whoever matches the nature of the problem.
knowledge_units.clinical_rationale_why: Refusal is a symptom with heterogeneous causes; routing depends on root cause, so diagnosis precedes assignment.
key_points: Severity drives escalation to staff meeting.
360° inquiry: physical vs neuropsychological vs combined.
Owner follows cause; plan revised only for durable change.
practice_rules: Step 1: escalate significant/repeated refusal to the team meeting.
Step 2: investigate physical causes and psychological causes together.
Step 3: assign to care staff (physical) or psychologist ± activity staff (psychological).
Step 4: revise the care plan only if the change persists.

knowledge_units.subtopic: Interviewer's proposed refusal metrics and workload realities
knowledge_units.interviewer_question: Could refusal be measured by task outcome: refused at first attempt, accepted at second attempt, or a definitive 'hard no' — and a resolution rate that excludes noise from the total task count?
knowledge_units.question_intent_why: She wants a denominator that reflects meaningful refusal events rather than all daily tasks.
knowledge_units.expert_answer: Expert input: carers are allocated roughly 8–12 residents per day; workload per resident varies by autonomy — e.g., of 8 residents, maybe 3 wash independently, 3 need encouragement/supervision, the rest need full help. Second attempts would be recorded; a definitive refusal may appear as a narrative note rather than a tick box.
knowledge_units.clinical_rationale_why: Task volume depends on each resident's autonomy, so raw task counts are poor denominators.
key_points: Typical allocation: ~8–12 residents per carer per day (example figure).
Autonomy levels: independent / needs encouragement or supervision / needs full help.
Hard refusals may only appear in free text.
practice_rules: Normalise refusal metrics by residents' autonomy level, not raw task counts.
knowledge_units.cautions_or_corrections: The resolution-rate formula is the interviewer's proposal, not an established clinical metric.

knowledge_units.subtopic: Strategies around refusal: staff swap and psychologist support
knowledge_units.interviewer_question: How would your proposed metric handle real refusal strategies?
knowledge_units.question_intent_why: She tested whether a per-staff metric captures how refusals are actually resolved.
knowledge_units.expert_answer: A refusal always has reasons, and the team always looks for strategies around it. Examples: (1) if it isn't working between a carer and a resident today (carer's mood, rapport), a colleague with whom it works better takes over and the task is done; (2) the carer calls the psychologist, who calms the situation so care can continue — the psychologist's action is itself important information. In the morning the psychologist has no assigned tasks so as to be available to the team.
knowledge_units.clinical_rationale_why: Rapport and the emotional climate of the interaction drive acceptance; flexible staffing and on-call psychological support are deliberate tools.
key_points: Staff substitution is a legitimate refusal strategy.
Psychologist acts as on-call de-escalation support, especially mornings.
Who resolved the refusal, and how, is clinically meaningful.
practice_rules: If a resident refuses with one carer, try a colleague with better rapport.
Call the psychologist to de-escalate before forcing care.
Document who intervened and what worked.

knowledge_units.subtopic: Qualify the refusal — not only its type but how it is expressed
knowledge_units.interviewer_question: Could refusals be labelled by type (hydration, medication, bathing) to add colour?
knowledge_units.question_intent_why: She was building a taxonomy by task domain.
knowledge_units.expert_answer: Beyond the type of refusal, the way it is expressed and experienced by the caregiver is central to the method: what staff see, witness and can write down. 'I don't want to eat today' is very different from throwing the plate in your face. Losing that information loses part of the approach.
knowledge_units.clinical_rationale_why: Manner and intensity of refusal indicate distress level and likely causes, guiding the response.
key_points: Record refusal domain AND manner/intensity.
Caregiver's observation of how refusal occurs is core data.
practice_rules: Always document how the refusal was expressed (verbal decline vs aggression).

knowledge_units.subtopic: Record timestamps reflect entry time, not event time
knowledge_units.interviewer_question: Could we measure time from task opening to completion?
knowledge_units.question_intent_why: She wanted an efficiency metric from timestamps.
knowledge_units.expert_answer: This is biased: staff may resolve something immediately but record it 12 hours later. Checking live, the expert confirmed timestamps are entry times — e.g., a physiotherapist's morning visit logged at 18:30; a lunchtime eating difficulty logged at 12:30.
knowledge_units.clinical_rationale_why: Batch documentation makes timestamps unreliable for timing analyses.
key_points: EHR timestamps = time of entry.
Time-to-resolution metrics are unreliable.
practice_rules: Don't infer event timing or delays from entry timestamps.

knowledge_units.subtopic: Severity and recurrence
knowledge_units.interviewer_question: What data on refusal severity would matter to you (e.g., refusal escalating into falls)? Would repeat refusal (>3 times/week for the same task) be useful?
knowledge_units.question_intent_why: She seeks indicators that matter to management and clinicians.
knowledge_units.expert_answer: There is an overall dependency profile per resident, and each case is looked at individually. For refusal, severity is considered but so is recurrence: occasional may be fine; daily refusal warrants investigation even if mild. Repetition itself is an indicator.
knowledge_units.clinical_rationale_why: Chronic low-grade refusal can signal an unmet need or a deteriorating situation as much as a single severe episode.
key_points: Both severity and frequency matter.
Mild but daily refusal triggers investigation.
practice_rules: Flag recurring refusals for review regardless of intensity.

knowledge_units.subtopic: Why refusal is an ideal lens on dementia care
knowledge_units.interviewer_question: Can we focus on refusal as the most universal pain point?
knowledge_units.question_intent_why: She wants a tractable focus.
knowledge_units.expert_answer: Refusal can originate from a very wide variety of reasons — e.g., refusing an activity because the person is tired, hungry or depressed. That makes it a window onto all aspects of what is happening with a person with dementia, which is why qualifying the refusal is essential: understanding it is how you enter the method.
knowledge_units.clinical_rationale_why: Refusal is a final common pathway for many unmet needs; decoding it touches every domain of care.
key_points: Refusal causes: fatigue, hunger, depression, pain, environment, rapport, and more.
Qualifying refusal is the entry point to the method's reasoning.
practice_rules: Treat each refusal as a question: what need is unmet?

knowledge_units.subtopic: Facility-level dependency averages and length of stay

knowledge_units.question_intent_why: She wanted a headline number showing the method's effect.
knowledge_units.expert_answer: Average dependency can be shared but is on a national scale (needs conversion); the MMSE is international. Average length of stay is short (2–3 years), so the facility average reflects a changing population — you cannot claim dependency was 'retained' because they are not the same people. knowledge_units.clinical_rationale_why: Population turnover confounds facility-level trends; cohort or within-person analysis is needed to attribute change.
key_points: Dependency scales are country-specific; MMSE is international.
Average length of stay ~2–3 years.
Facility averages mix different residents over time.
practice_rules: Use within-resident trajectories, not facility averages, to evaluate the method.

knowledge_units.subtopic: Physicians and therapists around the home
knowledge_units.interviewer_question: Can we interview general physicians and physiotherapists?
knowledge_units.question_intent_why: Mapping who is reachable and who holds clinical authority.
knowledge_units.expert_answer: Each home has one employed coordinating physician (sometimes part-time) who supervises care provision and hygiene; he is not a treating doctor. He coordinates all the doctors around a resident, organises care provision, gives opinions on treatments and behaviours, and — when nurses raise something — speaks to the treating doctors about adjusting treatment. Residents keep their own GPs/specialists, who visit them in the home as if at home; these are not employed and hard to reach. Physiotherapists are usually subcontractors but easier to reach. Doctor shortages mean some residents have no GP.
knowledge_units.clinical_rationale_why: Medical authority is distributed: treating doctors prescribe; the coordinating physician orchestrates; the home cannot direct external doctors.
key_points: Coordinating physician: coordinates, does not treat.
Treating GPs/specialists: external, visit residents.
Physiotherapists: usually subcontracted.
Some residents lack a GP.
practice_rules: Route treatment-change questions via nurses → coordinating physician → treating doctor.

knowledge_units.subtopic: Dementia care is harder than hotel-like facilities

knowledge_units.question_intent_why: Context on specialist dementia expertise.
knowledge_units.expert_answer: Markets are learning that dealing with dementia is more difficult than building a nice, hotel-like home; early on, stakeholders could not distinguish a general nursing home from a specialist dementia home. Public awareness of dementia does not mean knowing how to deal with it.
knowledge_units.clinical_rationale_why: Specialist dementia care is a clinical competence, not an amenity level.
key_points: Facility quality ≠ dementia-care competence.

knowledge_units.subtopic: Train-the-trainer dilution and local champions
knowledge_units.interviewer_question: What happened at the overseas hospital dementia unit?
knowledge_units.question_intent_why: Assess transferability.
knowledge_units.expert_answer: A public hospital set up a geriatric/dementia branch (patients, not residents) because it struggled with these patients (and to show local authorities it was acting). It was trained on and off for about a year — by local consultants who had themselves been trained by the method team: a diluted version passed down twice. Given limited budget and time, the result was satisfactory. The head nurse's commitment was a key driver.
knowledge_units.clinical_rationale_why: Each layer of cascade training loses fidelity; a motivated local clinical lead partly compensates.
key_points: Cascade training dilutes fidelity.
A committed head nurse is a key success factor.
About a year of intermittent training reached a satisfactory level.
practice_rules: When cascading training, identify and invest in a local clinical champion.

knowledge_units.subtopic: Constraints when exporting the method: no psychologists, no doctor access, no formal training
knowledge_units.interviewer_question: The knowledge core is orchestration between psychologist, physiotherapist, nurse, care aide and general doctor — can I see that in practice?
knowledge_units.question_intent_why: She wants to see role orchestration and transfer bottlenecks.
knowledge_units.expert_answer: Key constraints overseas: (1) no psychologists — social workers used as proxies, far from equivalent; (2) residents lack GPs; the medical side is handled by hospitals and operators cannot talk to residents' doctors; (3) no formal dementia-care training in nursing or medical schools, so everything must be taught from a low base.
knowledge_units.clinical_rationale_why: The method depends on psychological expertise and medical coordination; where these are absent, fidelity drops.
key_points: Psychologist role may need proxies (e.g., social workers) where unavailable.
Lack of physician access limits somatic rule-out and medication review.
Baseline training gaps require foundational teaching.
practice_rules: Assess availability of psychologists, physician access and baseline training before adapting the method.

knowledge_units.subtopic: Psychologist vs psychiatrist
knowledge_units.interviewer_question: (Interviewer said 'psychiatrist'.)
knowledge_units.question_intent_why: Terminology correction.
knowledge_units.expert_answer: Psychiatrists are doctors and prescribe drugs; psychologists are not doctors. There is overlap but they deal with different things. The method relies mostly on psychologists.
knowledge_units.clinical_rationale_why: Non-drug care is led by psychologists; prescribing remains medical.
key_points: Psychologists ≠ psychiatrists; only doctors prescribe.
Method primarily staffed with psychologists.
practice_rules: Use precise role terms.

knowledge_units.subtopic: Interviewer's model of role authority
knowledge_units.interviewer_question: (Interviewer explained her understanding to brief her product lead.)
knowledge_units.question_intent_why: Checking her mental model of hierarchy and authority.
knowledge_units.expert_answer: Interviewer's model: physicians are the only ones who prescribe and contribute the medical part of a care plan; the psychologist's role spans assessment to co-creating the care plan; care aides, nurses and field operations have distinct scopes. First-generation tooling should make specialists' work easier because frontline recording is inconsistent.
knowledge_units.clinical_rationale_why: Clarifying who decides what prevents tools from assigning tasks outside scope of practice.
key_points: Prescribing = physicians.
Psychologist: assessment → care-plan co-creation.
knowledge_units.cautions_or_corrections: Expert B (S13) clarified the care plan is built collegially by the whole team, not by physician–psychologist alone.

knowledge_units.subtopic: KPI framework: 3 outcome + 2 behaviour; sleep is not a behaviour
knowledge_units.interviewer_question: Behaviour KPIs: refusal, sleep time, wandering…?
knowledge_units.question_intent_why: Confirming the KPI structure.
knowledge_units.expert_answer: Expert corrected: sleep is not a behaviour. The framework is three health/outcome KPIs (antipsychotic medication use, weight loss, falls with major injury) and two behaviour KPIs (rejection of care/refusal and wandering), considering frequency and intensity.
knowledge_units.clinical_rationale_why: Keeping categories clean avoids mixing physiological measures with behavioural ones.
key_points: Outcome: antipsychotics, weight loss, falls with major injury.
Behaviour: refusal, wandering — frequency and intensity.
Sleep ≠ behaviour.

knowledge_units.subtopic: Use a comparison site
knowledge_units.interviewer_question: (Planning a site visit.)
knowledge_units.question_intent_why: Evaluation design.
knowledge_units.expert_answer: What you see at a partner site is only part of the method. Ideally also visit a home that does not apply the method, to compare.
knowledge_units.clinical_rationale_why: A comparator helps distinguish method effects from context.
key_points: Compare method vs non-method sites.
practice_rules: Include a non-adopting comparator in evaluations.

knowledge_units.subtopic: Frontline engagement after leadership change
knowledge_units.interviewer_question: Can we get frontline staff emotionally invested in the project?
knowledge_units.question_intent_why: Planning engagement.
knowledge_units.expert_answer: Expert: don't expect it. Since the founders left, teams turned over; newcomers were trained in the method but don't feel empowered by it or carry its legacy — they apply what they're told. Interviewer reframed: engage on practical pain points (easier days, fewer chaotic tasks) and the underused EHR. Expert: frontline staff have 'practical intelligence'.
knowledge_units.clinical_rationale_why: Method culture erodes with turnover; engagement must rest on day-to-day usefulness.
key_points: Turnover dilutes method culture.
Training without empowerment yields compliance, not ownership.
Frontline staff respond to practical relief.
practice_rules: Frame changes around reducing daily burden for frontline staff.

knowledge_units.subtopic: How expertise is transferred to a non-psychologist
knowledge_units.interviewer_question: How did the overseas consultant get trained in the method — classes?
knowledge_units.question_intent_why: Understanding knowledge-transfer pathways for an apprentice.
knowledge_units.expert_answer: Path: translating every course and document for years; online training with the method's neuropsychologist; 2–3 weeks of formal training; two weeks of field immersion in homes as a trainee — taking part in activities and staff meetings, running workshops, interviewing staff, interacting with residents, even living in a facility 24/7. She shows how far someone can master the method without being a psychologist — but some things only psychologists can do.
knowledge_units.clinical_rationale_why: Mastery comes from combining formal teaching with immersive, supervised practice; scope-of-practice limits remain.
key_points: Formal training + field immersion + supervision.
Non-psychologists can reach advanced operational mastery.
Some tasks reserved to psychologists.
practice_rules: Pair formal modules with immersion (activities, staff meetings, interviews).
Respect role boundaries for psychological assessment/intervention.

dialogue.speaker: INTERVIEWER
dialogue.text: At the overseas sites I visited (a public-hospital dementia unit and a private nursing home), two very different institutions appreciated the foundational principles and management philosophy of the method — a 'navigational map' for getting started. As expected, the data/scientific layer is not there yet; it is a long journey for a non-drug CBT-informed approach to reach clinical/scientific-grade recognition. I spoke with the head nurse, the operator/CEO and the social worker on site for about 90 minutes; it validated the framework and philosophy, and confirmed the data-driven layer is missing. I also spoke with the local consultant who has worked with the method for 6+ years… …she showed me the translated case-study workbook and the two booklets translated into the local language. The two biggest points are adaptability and compatibility: a solid set of care steps should be compatible and adaptable wherever it is applied, based on a systematic framework and formula — otherwise adoption costs in each new setting are too high. On site I saw the sensory stimulation room they assembled, the activity calendar plans, and the end of a workshop with the residents with dementia.

dialogue.speaker: EXPERT_A
dialogue.text: It's probably the lowest version you could experience of applying [THE METHOD] to a home that is not ours.

dialogue.speaker: EXPERT_A
dialogue.text: I think they've done an okay job, but it's probably the furthest away that we would expect from, you know, a nursing home we would work with directly in [COUNTRY_A].

dialogue.speaker: EXPERT_A
dialogue.text: So if you feel it already works to some extent there, then…

dialogue.speaker: EXPERT_A
dialogue.text: you know, it's encouraging.

dialogue.speaker: INTERVIEWER
dialogue.text: That's why it's a stress test of compatibility and adaptability — like a phone that must work in every country.

dialogue.speaker: EXPERT_A
dialogue.text: One thing's for sure: she's an expert, to the level we could bring her. She still lacks a lot of knowledge, but she's probably much better than the vast majority of people in that market when it comes to dementia care.

dialogue.speaker: EXPERT_A

knowledge_units.subtopic: Background of the method's clinical lead
knowledge_units.interviewer_question: Tell me about your background in delivering the CBT-informed method — training, tenure and role.
knowledge_units.question_intent_why: Establish the informant's expertise and vantage point.
knowledge_units.expert_answer: Expert B is a neuropsychologist (Master's 2), first introduced to CBT during training; worked as in-house neuropsychologist in two homes (including opening one) for several years; now operational and scientific director of the method — guarantor of the approach in the homes, supervising psychologists and to some extent activity staff, and consultant/trainer for client homes and home care; he has also trained and supervised overseas consultants online.
knowledge_units.clinical_rationale_why: Knowing the informant's role helps weight their statements (clinical lead vs executive).
key_points: Neuropsychology specialisation.
Roles: in-house clinician → method director/supervisor/trainer.

knowledge_units.subtopic: Three pillars of the in-house psychologist role
knowledge_units.interviewer_question: (Expert B added detail on his former role.)
knowledge_units.question_intent_why: Defines the psychologist's scope in the method.
knowledge_units.expert_answer: Three elements: (1) residents — psychological support and running therapeutic workshops; (2) team — helping staff face difficulties and training them on the job in dementia competencies; (3) families — supporting them in their distress, facilitating communication with their relative, regular group sessions, smoothing family–home relations.
knowledge_units.clinical_rationale_why: Dementia care outcomes depend on the resident, the care team and the family system together.
key_points: Residents: support + therapeutic workshops.
Team: support + on-the-job training.
Families: support + communication facilitation.
practice_rules: Plan psychologist time across residents, staff and families.

knowledge_units.subtopic: Expertise comes from mentorship and trial-and-error
knowledge_units.interviewer_question: (Expert B on how he learned.)
knowledge_units.question_intent_why: Reveals how expertise is built — relevant for an AI apprentice.
knowledge_units.expert_answer: No further formal CBT training after university; expertise comes mainly from mentorship by the method's originator and from trial and error with residents — learning from successes and errors.
knowledge_units.clinical_rationale_why: Applied CBT in dementia is a practice skill refined through supervised experience and reflection on outcomes.
key_points: Mentorship + reflective practice > additional coursework.
practice_rules: Capture successes and failures as learning cases.

knowledge_units.subtopic: What CBT-informed care in dementia aims to do
knowledge_units.interviewer_question: (Prompted by the problem set 'difficulty tracking treatment effectiveness'.)
knowledge_units.question_intent_why: Expert B reframed the premise before ranking.
knowledge_units.expert_answer: Fundamentally, the approach offers an environment that brings quality of life and slows the disease, through cognitive stimulation and the human, physical and social environment. 'Improving symptoms' applies when there are behavioural disorders; but the disease is not curable and there will be no significant improvement in, e.g., cognition. Cognitive impairments do not necessarily lead to behavioural issues. The aim is the most comfortable and peaceful life possible — not only managing behaviour. 'Treatment' is the wrong word.
knowledge_units.clinical_rationale_why: Setting goals as quality of life and slowing decline avoids judging the approach by impossible cognitive gains.
key_points: Goals: quality of life, slowing decline, comfort, peace.
Means: cognitive stimulation + adapted human/physical/social environment.
Do not expect cognitive improvement.
Avoid the word 'treatment'.
practice_rules: Frame outcomes as quality of life and behaviour, not cognitive recovery.

knowledge_units.subtopic: Ranking the six problem sets; personalised plans at scale
knowledge_units.interviewer_question: Do you agree with the six problem sets, and how would you rank them (must-have / nice-to-have / not important)?
knowledge_units.question_intent_why: Prioritise what a support tool should address.
knowledge_units.expert_answer: Indispensable (must-have): (1) tracking effectiveness, (2) personalised care plans for everyone, (4) continuous staff training. Hardest to achieve: (3) inconsistent performance of interventions and (5) inconsistent frontline delivery — because they depend on teams' initial training and number of professionals, which differ in every facility. On personalisation: you cannot fix one 'treatment' for everyone — every patient is different even within a common methodology. A personalised plan for every resident is a near-mandatory prerequisite built on the initial assessment and life-history collection; it is not 'easy or hard' — it takes time, so at scale it is difficult.
knowledge_units.clinical_rationale_why: Individualisation is the core of the approach; scale problems are about time and staffing, not about whether to individualise.
key_points: Must-have: effectiveness tracking, personalised plans, continuous training.
Hardest: consistency of interventions and frontline delivery.
Personalised plan = prerequisite; depends on initial assessment + life history.
Variability driven by staffing and baseline training.
practice_rules: Never standardise the plan itself — standardise the methodology for building it.
Budget time for initial assessment and life-history collection.

knowledge_units.subtopic: Creating psychological safety for the informant
knowledge_units.interviewer_question: (Interviewer/translator framing.)
knowledge_units.question_intent_why: Encourage candid answers.
knowledge_units.expert_answer: The informant was told there are no right or wrong answers and he need not agree to please; the interviewer positioned herself as a listener ('I'm your psychologist today').
knowledge_units.clinical_rationale_why: Reducing social-desirability bias yields more accurate tacit knowledge.
key_points: State that there are no right answers.
Invite disagreement explicitly.
practice_rules: Open elicitation with explicit permission to disagree.

knowledge_units.subtopic: One-month integration review after admission
knowledge_units.interviewer_question: How do you address tracking effectiveness day to day?
knowledge_units.question_intent_why: Learn the actual evaluation workflow.
knowledge_units.expert_answer: An integration review one month after admission shows how the person is integrating and whether symptoms have improved — orientation, socialisation, weight/eating, sleep. The initial plan is built from extensive pre-admission information (life history, neuropsychological profile, abilities) and is usually adjusted at this point. After that, effectiveness is assessed through the personalised care plan: objectives are set and evaluated at defined times. Done by the multidisciplinary team with the family and the resident where able.
knowledge_units.clinical_rationale_why: Admission is a high-risk transition; a structured early review catches poor adaptation and corrects initial assumptions.
key_points: Pre-admission: life history, neuropsychological profile, abilities.
1-month integration review: orientation, socialisation, eating/weight, sleep, symptoms.
Ongoing: objective-based evaluation in the PCP.
Involve family/resident.
practice_rules: Schedule an integration review at ~1 month post-admission.
Revise the initial plan based on observed integration.

knowledge_units.subtopic: Care-plan objectives as testable hypotheses
knowledge_units.interviewer_question: (Expert B example.)
knowledge_units.question_intent_why: Shows how objectives are set and evaluated.
knowledge_units.expert_answer: If someone likes music, the plan may set participation in two (2–3) music workshops a week and monitor effects on mood, socialisation and participation. If someone stays in their room and is low, the objective is socialisation, checked at several points (leaving the room more, joining groups). Objectives are educated assumptions from pre-admission and admission information; if no effect, the strategy is reassessed.
knowledge_units.clinical_rationale_why: Person-centred objectives are hypotheses about what will improve wellbeing; observation confirms or refutes them.
key_points: Use preferences (e.g., music) to set concrete, frequency-based objectives.
Withdrawn/low mood → socialisation objective.
Re-evaluate and adjust if no effect.
practice_rules: Write objectives with frequency and an observable outcome.
Review at set intervals; change strategy if ineffective.

knowledge_units.subtopic: Measuring effectiveness for refusals and behaviours
knowledge_units.interviewer_question: (Continuing on tracking effectiveness.)
knowledge_units.question_intent_why: Defines success criteria.
knowledge_units.expert_answer: Describe the refusal, put a strategy in place, and see whether it works: success = refusal eliminated or fewer refusals than baseline (per day/week/month depending on usual frequency). For behaviours: does it continue, more/less frequent, more/less acute? Without drugs, strategies target behavioural disorders and are judged by whether the behaviour stops.
knowledge_units.clinical_rationale_why: Baseline-relative change in frequency/intensity is the practical effectiveness measure.
key_points: Describe → strategy → measure vs baseline.
Reduction counts as success, not only elimination.
Track frequency and acuity.
practice_rules: Record a baseline frequency before introducing a strategy.
Choose the time unit to match the behaviour's usual frequency.

knowledge_units.subtopic: Consistent principles, flexible form
knowledge_units.interviewer_question: (Problem set 3: inconsistent performance across facilities.)
knowledge_units.question_intent_why: What must be standardised vs left local.
knowledge_units.expert_answer: Differences between facilities are normal (many variables). What matters for generalising is that core care principles are active in every facility — cognitive stimulation, the approach to families, a CBT approach to behavioural disorders, genuine therapeutic activities — with the same methodology. Each home having its own personality is fine. Example (Expert A): a music therapeutic workshop can take many forms (listening, playing instruments) as long as it follows the technical guide and aims at multi-area brain stimulation; staff must understand why they do things.
knowledge_units.clinical_rationale_why: Fidelity is to mechanisms and principles, not surface procedures; understanding the 'why' enables safe local variation.
key_points: Standardise principles and methodology, not form.
Therapeutic activities need a technical guide and a stimulation rationale.
Staff must understand the purpose behind actions.
practice_rules: Audit whether principles are 'alive', not whether scripts are copied.
Teach the rationale with every activity guide.

knowledge_units.subtopic: Psychologist at every handover + regular flash trainings
knowledge_units.interviewer_question: How is continuous staff training addressed day to day?
knowledge_units.question_intent_why: Learn the training workflow.
knowledge_units.expert_answer: The psychologist should be present at all daily handovers, explaining certain deviant behaviours and re-explaining the disease (informal, ongoing training). An internal training plan adds regular short 'flash' trainings (monthly or quarterly) by the psychologist, the coordinating nurse or the coordinating physician on topics such as behavioural disorders and eating disorders.
knowledge_units.clinical_rationale_why: Just-in-time explanation at handover links theory to the residents staff are caring for that day.
key_points: Psychologist attends daily handovers.
Regular flash trainings by psychologist / coordinating nurse / coordinating physician.
practice_rules: Use handovers to explain behaviours in terms of the disease.
Maintain a rolling programme of short trainings.

knowledge_units.subtopic: Barriers to training attendance
knowledge_units.interviewer_question: What is hard about this in practice? (invitation to vent)
knowledge_units.question_intent_why: Surface real-world pain points.
knowledge_units.expert_answer: Mobilising the whole team is hard: taking carers off the floor for an afternoon leaves fewer on the floor; staffing gaps or residents needing more care mean poor attendance; trying to train everyone becomes exhausting. Short videos to watch often could help replicate training — but it is uncertain staff would use them.
knowledge_units.clinical_rationale_why: Training competes with care time; formats must fit around staffing constraints.
key_points: Attendance limited by staffing and acuity.
Micro-learning (short videos) is an option with uncertain uptake.
practice_rules: Offer short, repeatable formats alongside live sessions.

knowledge_units.subtopic: Poor handover notes and the 'no news' bias
knowledge_units.interviewer_question: (Expert B on tracking difficulties.)
knowledge_units.question_intent_why: Explains why effectiveness is hard to see in records.
knowledge_units.expert_answer: Main difficulty for following the personalised plan and judging effectiveness: care assistants' handover notes are often poor, so it is hard to synthesise a success. Staff write fairly complete notes when there are difficulties (e.g., a resident impossible to approach is noted daily) but don't write when things go well — so when a resident improves, notes stop, and you can't tell whether nothing happened, they forgot, or there was improvement.
knowledge_units.clinical_rationale_why: Negativity-biased documentation hides successes and makes improvement invisible.
key_points: Handover-note quality limits evaluation.
Problems documented; improvements not.
Absence of notes is ambiguous.
practice_rules: Explicitly prompt staff to document improvements and successes.
Treat 'no entries' as unknown, not as resolved.

knowledge_units.subtopic: Critique of the KPI set; add apathy and depression
knowledge_units.interviewer_question: How do you feel about these KPIs as effectiveness measures (antipsychotic use, falls with serious injury, weight loss; refusal, wandering, sleep disorders)?
knowledge_units.question_intent_why: Validate indicators with the clinical lead.
knowledge_units.expert_answer: Antipsychotic medication use: yes. Weight loss: a hugely important indicator in Alzheimer's — it tells a lot. Falls with serious injury: not a real indicator — falls depend on many factors (residents who walk/wander more may even fall less). Refusal, sleep disorders and wandering: agree. Missing: level of apathy and level of depression — people with Alzheimer's are (almost) all depressed; the method aims to be a natural antidepressant. Apathy is often not addressed by homes and is an entry point to further decline and later behavioural issues.
knowledge_units.clinical_rationale_why: Indicators should reflect the method's mechanism (mood, engagement); falls are multifactorial and can be confounded by mobility.
key_points: Keep: antipsychotic use, weight, refusal, wandering, sleep disorders.
Question: falls with major injury as an indicator.
Add: apathy and depression.
practice_rules: Include mood (depression) and apathy measures in any evaluation.
Interpret falls cautiously; don't penalise mobility.

knowledge_units.subtopic: How psychologist and physician coordinate: the collegial care-plan meeting
knowledge_units.interviewer_question: Is there a standard meeting where psychologist and physician orchestrate?
knowledge_units.question_intent_why: Correct her assumption of a physician–psychologist dyad.
knowledge_units.expert_answer: No dedicated dyad meeting. There is a specific personalised-care-plan meeting — collegial: physician, psychologist, sometimes the director, a nurse, a care assistant, sometimes the family. It centralises all resident information and sets objectives; the psychologist records them in the care plan, and care is continuous with revisions in further multidisciplinary meetings. Some homes add a monthly psychologist–coordinating-physician check-in on behavioural difficulties (what works, what doesn't), but it is not required — the care plan belongs to the whole team. Use 'personalised care plan', not 'treatment'.
knowledge_units.clinical_rationale_why: Behaviour and wellbeing are shaped by every role; shared ownership prevents siloed decisions.
key_points: PCP meeting is multidisciplinary, may include family.
Psychologist documents objectives.
Optional monthly psych–physician review of behavioural cases.
Terminology: personalised care plan.
practice_rules: Convene the PCP meeting with all relevant roles and, where possible, family.
Review behavioural cases regularly with the coordinating physician.

knowledge_units.subtopic: Refusal typology: interaction-driven and internal/environmental causes
knowledge_units.interviewer_question: We classified refusals as Type 1 (refusal of standard care, e.g., medication) and Type 2 (refusal after staff intervene on an observed behaviour, e.g., trying to leave). Do you agree?
knowledge_units.question_intent_why: Validate her taxonomy.
knowledge_units.expert_answer: Type 1 is not wrong, but it can't be called refusal of the 'CBT intervention': refusals during washing etc. happen because staff aren't applying the approach properly — it's the staff–resident interaction, not the approach, that generates refusal. Type 2 is missing internal and environmental causes: too much noise, pain, something frightening, hallucinations.
knowledge_units.clinical_rationale_why: Refusals are often iatrogenic (caused by how care is delivered) or driven by internal/environmental triggers, which must be in the taxonomy.
key_points: Many refusals reflect care-delivery style.
Add internal causes (pain, hallucinations) and environmental causes (noise, fear).
practice_rules: When a refusal occurs, first review how the care was approached.
Check environment (noise) and internal states (pain, hallucination).

knowledge_units.subtopic: Elopement is not refusal — it signals poor integration
knowledge_units.interviewer_question: Anything to change in the list of behaviours linked to refusal?
knowledge_units.question_intent_why: Refine categories.
knowledge_units.expert_answer: Agree with the list except elopement (running away), which is not a cause of refusal and arguably not even a behavioural disorder or impulsive behaviour like wandering; it reflects general unease. It is seen mostly in newcomers who are disoriented and don't know where they are; it tends to fade over time. When residents want to run away, it means they are not integrated into the home — the response is broad: rework the resident's integration (whereas refusals call for more targeted actions).
knowledge_units.clinical_rationale_why: Exit-seeking early after admission expresses disorientation and lack of belonging; integration work addresses the cause.
key_points: Elopement ≠ refusal; ≠ wandering.
Common in newcomers; linked to disorientation; fades.
Response: strengthen integration.
practice_rules: For exit-seeking, review and intensify the integration plan.
Expect higher elopement risk in the first weeks after admission.

knowledge_units.subtopic: Escalation ladder: add frequency/habituality
knowledge_units.interviewer_question: Please review the triggers list (incl. night-time) and the escalation ladder (Q11–12).
knowledge_units.question_intent_why: Systematise how interventions are triggered.
knowledge_units.expert_answer: Sequence discussed: a symptom appears → identify it → measure it → plan a strategy → apply → measure again. Expert B noted something missing: frequency — whether the behaviour is habitual or not.
knowledge_units.clinical_rationale_why: Whether a behaviour is new or habitual changes its meaning and urgency.
key_points: Escalation: identify → measure → strategy → apply → re-measure.
Add habituality/frequency as a dimension.
practice_rules: Classify each behaviour as habitual vs new before escalating.

knowledge_units.subtopic: Missing strategies: environment and preventive bodily care
knowledge_units.interviewer_question: Any other operational comments?
knowledge_units.question_intent_why: Complete the strategy list.
knowledge_units.expert_answer: Missing from strategies: environmental adaptation — hugely important (routines, stimulation, integration, socialisation) — and preventive care of bodily health, which is part of the methodology.
knowledge_units.clinical_rationale_why: Environment and physical health are primary levers for behaviour and wellbeing.
key_points: Environmental adaptation is a core strategy.
Preventive physical health care is part of the method.
practice_rules: Include environmental adjustments and routines in every behavioural plan.
Maintain preventive health checks as behaviour prevention.

knowledge_units.subtopic: Body and mind: rule out somatic causes first
knowledge_units.interviewer_question: (Expert A elaborating on Expert B's point.)
knowledge_units.question_intent_why: Key clinical heuristic.
knowledge_units.expert_answer: Before blaming the disease, rule out anything somatic or basic needs: a sore thumb, wrong footwear, hunger. Check sensory aids — a resident 'refusing' may simply not hear you (no hearing aids) or not be wearing glasses. Expert A recalled internal findings that about half of behavioural issues are triggered by health/body-related issues; if you don't rule that out first, you miss the point most of the time.
knowledge_units.clinical_rationale_why: Unrecognised pain, discomfort, unmet needs and sensory deficits are common drivers of behaviour in people who cannot verbalise them.
key_points: Rule out pain, discomfort, hunger, footwear, etc.
Check hearing aids and glasses before labelling refusal.
Somatic causes reportedly account for a large share of behaviours.
practice_rules: Run a somatic/basic-needs and sensory check before any behavioural interpretation.
knowledge_units.cautions_or_corrections: The ~50% figure is the expert's recollection of internal findings, not a cited study.

knowledge_units.subtopic: Selecting informants for practitioner interviews
knowledge_units.interviewer_question: Could we interview a psychologist, a head/coordinating nurse and a care aide or activity coordinator?
knowledge_units.question_intent_why: Plan next elicitation round.
knowledge_units.expert_answer: Prefer long-tenured staff who know the homes well (e.g., an experienced head nurse; an activity coordinator who is also an art therapist with dementia-specific training). Newly hired psychologists are less useful informants; experienced ones were on leave. Interviews must be short (≤30 min) because staff cannot be kept off the floor.
knowledge_units.clinical_rationale_why: Tacit knowledge resides in experienced practitioners; time-boxing respects care continuity.
key_points: Choose experienced informants.
Limit interviews to ~30 minutes.
practice_rules: Prioritise experienced staff; keep sessions short.
