dialogue.text: On peut dire aussi peut être que ça pourrait l'aider, que les soignants ont tendance à faire des. Des transmissions assez complètes lorsqu'il y a des difficultés. Pour autant, ils ne transcrivent pas forcément à l'écrit quand ça se passe bien ou quand il y a une réussite. C'estàdire que si [RESIDENT], il est impossible de l'approcher, on va noter tous les jours, puis, quand ça va aller mieux, on va plus faire de transmission et du coup, on a du mal à voir finalement l'efficacité parce qu'il n'y a plus rien.
dialogue.english_translation: It may also help to say that carers tend to write fairly complete notes when there are difficulties, but they don't necessarily write anything when things go well or when there's a success. So if [RESIDENT] is impossible to approach, it gets noted every day; then when things improve, there are no more notes — and it's hard to see effectiveness because there's nothing left.

dialogue.speaker: EXPERT_A
dialogue.text: Mm-hmm. on. Mmm. Okay, so one of the difficulties that we have is that whenever there's a problem. there will be a record of it most of the time. And if you get a refusal or behavior problem every day, then they'll probably be written down every day. but. As and when things improve, they tend to write less. Because if there's nothing wrong, they won't say it. So, if you get a refusal every day, and then suddenly that person improves and stops refusing, then the staff won't write, well, she's refusing less. He just wants anything. Which, uh, which makes it difficult to assess. the effectiveness of what we do, because you don't know if nothing's written because they forgot, or because there was no improvement, or what's so. There's no active, there's no active recording of improvement, not enough anyway.

dialogue.speaker: INTERVIEWER
dialogue.text: Super helpful. That's a good segue into more technical questions — less about his pain points and more about aligning the technicalities of the product with him.

dialogue.speaker: EXPERT_A
dialogue.text: Okay, donc du coup, on va sortir un peu de l'exploitation de l'opérationnel, et l'idée, c'est de rentrer un peu dans le détail du produit justement et les aspects techniques de comment ça pourrait fonctionner. Pour s'assurer que. Ce qu'ils envisagent de développer correspond à ce qui peut être utile.
dialogue.english_translation: We'll now leave operations and go into the detail of the product and its technical aspects, to make sure what they plan to build matches what's useful.

dialogue.speaker: INTERVIEWER
dialogue.text: First, the KPIs — how does he feel about this set of KPIs as measures of effectiveness?

dialogue.speaker: INTERVIEWER
dialogue.text: Around, I would say, effectiveness. Yeah.

dialogue.speaker: EXPERT_A
dialogue.text: Donc, si on prend un peu les thématiques, on a évoqué plus tôt. Et que on essaie de mesurer un peu. Finalement, ces approches par les trois indicateurs qui sont listés là. C'est à dire l'usage des médicaments, des antipsychotiques, les chutes avec blessures graves et la perte de poids, la courbe de poids. Um, donc ça c'est pour les aspects. Ouais, soin entre guillemets et pour le comportement, euh, le refus, donc nombre de refus, fréquence, etc. Les rances et les troubles du sommeil. Est ce que vous pensez que si on utilise ces indicateurs comme élément de mesure, finalement de. De l'évolution favorable de l'application de la méthode. On se. On est dans le juste. Ou ça va pas nous permettre de mesurer les points qui sont importants qu'on a mentionné plus haut.
dialogue.english_translation: So, taking the themes we mentioned earlier… …and trying to measure these approaches with the three indicators listed: use of antipsychotic medication, falls with serious injury, and weight loss / the weight curve — those are for the care aspects. For behaviour: refusal — number of refusals, frequency, etc. … …wandering and sleep disorders. Do you think that if we use these indicators to measure favourable progress from applying the method, we're on target — or will they fail to capture the important points mentioned earlier?

dialogue.speaker: EXPERT_B
dialogue.text: L'usage des médicaments antipsychotiques. Oui, la perte de poids, c'est un capiat hyper important, la maladie d'alzheimer, parce qu'elle nous dit beaucoup de choses. En revanche, les chutes avec blessures graves. Je vois pas trop. À quoi ça sert? Parce que. Les chutes sont dépendantes des choses, alors si effectivement il déambulent, plus il chutent moins, mais je pense pas que ça soit un vrai indicateur.
dialogue.english_translation: Antipsychotic medication use — yes. Weight loss is a hugely important KPI in Alzheimer's because it tells us a lot. On the other hand, falls with serious injury — I don't really see the point, because falls depend on many things; if they walk/wander more, they may actually fall less — I don't think it's a real indicator.

dialogue.speaker: EXPERT_A
dialogue.text: Okay, so [EXPERT_B] is saying that the use of neuroleptics, uh… And, weight management, absolutely key. And especially with Alzheimer's, the, you know, weight provision is very important. And antipsychotic as well, of course. But when it comes to falls. Uh, with major injury in addition, uh, he doesn't really see the point.

dialogue.speaker: INTERVIEWER
dialogue.text: Okay, yeah, sure. And on a refusal wondering, I guess. It feels the same, right? That this quite standard. symptoms, behavior symptoms.

dialogue.speaker: EXPERT_B
dialogue.text: Ouais refus, je suis d'accord. Les troubles du sommeil aussi les rances, aussi mais ce qui est important aussi dans la maladie. C'est le niveau d'apathie, surtout avec la méthode [OPERATOR] et le niveau de dépression, sachant qu'ils sont tous dépressifs. Les Alzheimer. A la base. Notre projet, c'est d'avoir un antidépresseur naturel, donc on pourrait mettre des dépressions et apathie.
dialogue.english_translation: Refusal — I agree. Sleep disorders too, and wandering too. But what's also important in the disease is the level of apathy — especially with [THE METHOD] — and the level of depression, given that people with Alzheimer's are all depressed. Fundamentally our aim is to be a natural antidepressant, so we could add depression and apathy.

dialogue.speaker: EXPERT_A
dialogue.text: Okay, so he's agreeing on all the KPIs for behavior. But he feels that there are two important ones that are missing, and they would relate to apathy. and depression.

dialogue.speaker: INTERVIEWER
dialogue.text: What's the other one?

dialogue.speaker: EXPERT_A
dialogue.text: Depression. Because all Alzheimer patients have are depressed. And apathy is something usually nursing homes don't deal with, and is the entry point into. to disease and further down the line behavior issues.

dialogue.speaker: INTERVIEWER
dialogue.text: Next: how do the psychologist and the physician orchestrate with each other? It sounds like there's a standard meeting between them?

dialogue.speaker: EXPERT_A
dialogue.text: Between a psychologist and a doctor?

dialogue.speaker: EXPERT_A
dialogue.text: I'll ask him, but I don't think so. [EXPERT_B], est-ce qu'est-ce qu'est-ce qu'est-ce qu'est-ce qu.
dialogue.english_translation: I'll ask him, but I don't think so. (asks in French)

dialogue.speaker: EXPERT_B
dialogue.text: Non, justement ici, c'est plutôt on va parler plutôt de de l'étude de cas. Euh, non pardon. La réunion, il y a une réunion spécifique. Projet d'accompagnement personnalisé. Où, justement, on va centraliser toutes les données du résident, on va déterminer les objectifs et c'est le psy qui va les inscrire dans les soins, mais en fait, le traitement continu. On va dire: c'est une réunion, une réunion. Collégiale avec Médecins Psy, parfois directeur, une infirmière, une aide-soignante et parfois même la famille.
dialogue.english_translation: No — rather, there's a specific meeting: the personalized care plan meeting. That's where we centralize all the resident's information and set the objectives, and it's the psychologist who records them in the care plan — but the care is continuous. It's a collegial meeting with the physician, the psychologist, sometimes the director, a nurse, a care assistant, and sometimes even the family.

dialogue.speaker: EXPERT_A
dialogue.text: Okay, so there's no specific one-on-one meeting between the doctor and the psychologist. Psychologists will sit in a multidisciplinary team to write. the the personalized care plan. And then he will record it into the software. Okay, and then, uh, they are… along the way again. You know, revisions of that plan and multidisciplinary meetings to review it. And sometimes the the relatives are. Taking part as well.

dialogue.speaker: EXPERT_B
dialogue.text: Well. Pour donner un exemple psychologue, médecin, mais c'est mon exemple. Par exemple, sur un établissement, on faisait un point une fois par mois avec le médecin Co. De l'établissement pour justement faire un point de suivi de où on en était sur les difficultés avec les troubles du comportement. Et voir ce qui marche et ce qui marche pas, mais c'est pas une obligation dans la méthode [OPERATOR] et surtout de que le projet d'accompagnement, c'est toute l'équipe, c'est pas forcément si elle est médecin.
dialogue.english_translation: To give an example of psychologist–physician coordination — my own example: in one facility we held a monthly check-in with the coordinating physician to review where we were on behavioural difficulties and see what was working and what wasn't. But that's not a requirement of the method; above all, the care plan is the whole team's, not necessarily the physician's.

dialogue.speaker: EXPERT_A
dialogue.text: Hmm. So he was saying that in one of the homes he worked at she did have regular meetings with the doctor, but it's not an obligation, and in any case the [OPERATOR] method. Requires more multidisciplinary team meetings rather than just, you know, a duo of the doctor and the psychologist. Everyone should be involved. And also in what you write, you should really stop using treatment as a word. It's the wrong word. It's it's not a treatment.

dialogue.speaker: INTERVIEWER
dialogue.text: Okay, care plan. Care plan.

dialogue.speaker: EXPERT_A
dialogue.text: It's, yeah, it's a personalized care plan. That's what we call it.

dialogue.speaker: INTERVIEWER
dialogue.text: Now the refusal types. We bucketed refusals into two types and listed the main refusal types and associated behaviours in this table. The key is to differentiate the hierarchy and the types of refusal.

dialogue.speaker: EXPERT_A
dialogue.text: But how do you… how do you… What belongs to type one? What belongs to type two in your class?

dialogue.speaker: INTERVIEWER
dialogue.text: Type 1 is refusal of standard care delivery and intervention (e.g., refusing medication — a routine refusal of assistance). Type 2 is refusal triggered by a staff observation (e.g., staff see the resident trying to leave the premises and intervene).

dialogue.speaker: EXPERT_A
dialogue.text: Right. Okay. Euh, ok, alors du coup, la question [EXPERT_B], c'est. Ils ont identifié. Enfin, ils ont classé les refus en deux catégories. La première catégorie. C'est dans le cadre de l'activité normale du quotidien et toutes les tâches qu'on doit accomplir auprès du résident. Lui donner ses médicaments, lui donner à manger, l'aider à se laver, etc. C'est le premier type et le deuxième type qu'ils ont identifié, c'est. En gros, quand le personnel constate. Quelque chose que fait le résident qu'ils essaient d'intervenir et que, du coup, le résident refuse finalement de. D'obtempérer ou de. Tu y réussiras. Dire ma phrase, à pas contrôler, mais à corriger son son comportement.
dialogue.english_translation: They've classified refusals into two categories. The first is within normal daily activity and all the tasks we do for the resident — giving medication, feeding, helping with washing, etc. The second is when staff notice something the resident is doing, try to intervene, and the resident refuses to comply — not to control but to correct the behaviour.

dialogue.speaker: EXPERT_B
dialogue.text: Really. Oui, juste du coup, par exemple, sur la traduction, c'est marqué face à la prestation de soins et à l'intervention des Tcc. Alors ok, il y a des refus sur la toilette et autres, mais c'est pas, c'est parce qu'ils utilisent pas les Tcc qui est normalement une bonne méthode. Et après oui, le refus par une autre observation, ça peut être qu'il y ait trop de bruit dans la salle, qu'il y ait une douleur, etc, et qui est plutôt interne aux résidents ou à l'environnement.
dialogue.english_translation: On the translation, it says 'refusal in response to care delivery and CBT intervention'. OK, there are refusals during washing and so on — but that's because they're not using the CBT approach, which is normally the right method. And yes, refusal from 'another observation' could be too much noise in the room, pain, etc. — causes that are internal to the resident or environmental.

dialogue.speaker: EXPERT_A
dialogue.text: Alright, okay. Okay, so what [EXPERT_B] is saying is that, um, the way the first one is labeled is not… wrong in itself, except you can't really say Cbt intervention. Uh, because it's because you don't use CBT that you get refusals. So it's not the CBT in itself, uh, that is generating refusal, but it's the staff interaction with the residents. that is not doing it in the right way. So it's 1st comment. And the second comment is. Type 2 is not wrong, but it's missing also internal and environmental causes. Say, for example, all of a sudden that there's a there's a very loud noise. But there's something going on that frightens the the resident. Um… That's, you know, that's something that is not directly linked to the daily care delivery or the observation. It's external factors or. If you know the person has a hallucination, or whatever.

dialogue.speaker: INTERVIEWER
dialogue.text: We'll refine the table. Anything missing or to change, beyond the two comments he just made?

dialogue.speaker: EXPERT_B
dialogue.text: Oui, je suis d'accord avec avec tout, euh, sauf les fugues qui sont pas un élément, une cause en tout cas de de refus. La la fugue, elle est, elle est autre chose. Donc, hormis la ligne Fugue, c'est à peu près les principaux types que l'on que l'on a. Au quotidien.
dialogue.english_translation: Yes, I agree with all of it, except elopement/running away, which isn't a cause of refusal — it's something else. Apart from the elopement row, these are roughly the main types we see day to day.

dialogue.speaker: EXPERT_A
dialogue.text: Okay, so he's saying that he agrees to most of your list, except for elopement, that in his eyes. Is not refusal, it's something else. It has other causes, and um. It's. Yeah, he wouldn't put it in that category.

dialogue.speaker: INTERVIEWER
dialogue.text: Elopement is something else then — what category would it be?

dialogue.speaker: EXPERT_B
dialogue.text: Euh, la fugue. Euh, c'est, c'est même pas un trouble du comportement, je dirais. C'est même pas du comportement impulsif, comme de la déambulation. Je sais même pas d'ailleurs, c'est une bonne question, mais mais c'est pas un refus. La fugue. Je pense que c'était un mal être. I mean, it's general, mais euh. C'est pas une cause de refus. En tout cas.
dialogue.english_translation: Elopement — I'd say it's not even a behavioural disorder. It's not even impulsive behaviour like wandering. I don't actually know — good question — but it's not a refusal. I think it reflects a general sense of unease/distress. It's not a cause of refusal, anyway.

dialogue.speaker: EXPERT_A
dialogue.text: So he's confirming that that's not a refusal in his eyes. He wouldn't really know where to put it. It's not a behavior issue either. Not really.

dialogue.speaker: EXPERT_B
dialogue.text: À la rigueur, ils pourraient refuser tout un tas de trucs parce qu'ils ont pas envie d'être dans dans. Dans l'nursing home (EHPAD) dans l'établissement. Je pense qu'il. Mais c'est souvent parce qu'ils sont complètement désorientés, ils savent pas bien où ils sont, donc on peut avoir des refus sur ça, mais c'est quand même très au début. Généralement, ils veulent fuguer en arrivant après, ça s'estompe quand même un peu. Un peu, donc.
dialogue.english_translation: At most, they might refuse all sorts of things because they don't want to be in the home. But it's often because they're completely disoriented and don't know where they are, so you can get refusals around that — but it's very early on. Generally they want to run away on arrival, and then it fades somewhat.

dialogue.speaker: EXPERT_A
dialogue.text: All right. So, he's saying that, um… Elopement is something we witness mostly with newcomers. And it tends to disappear with time. It's just that most of the time they're lost, they don't really, you know, they have difficulty adapting to a new environment. They don't understand where they are, why they're there. And they tried to escape. Um, so it's a, it's a, it's a symptom in itself that is linked to. disorientation most of the time.

dialogue.speaker: EXPERT_B
dialogue.text: Et ce que j'ai appris, c'est que quand ils veulent fuguer, c'est qu'ils sont pas intégrés dans l'établissement, donc c'est beaucoup plus large comme action de retravailler l'intégration du résident alors que le refus on va. Même avoir des choses. Moins global. En tout cas.
dialogue.english_translation: What I've learned is that when they want to run away, it's because they're not integrated into the home — so the action is much broader: rework the resident's integration. Whereas with refusal, the actions are more targeted.

dialogue.speaker: EXPERT_A
dialogue.text: People are saying that what he's witnessed is that people trying to escape, to elope. are very often people who are not sufficiently integrated into their home. And the work we would then do to, you know, stop them wanting to escape. Would be to work again harder on the integration of the resin, and that's definitely not something. That is what you see with refusal. It's just not the same approach, same strategy at all.

dialogue.speaker: INTERVIEWER
dialogue.text: For the rest — the questions on triggers, i.e., what prompts a point-of-care intervention in the CBT-informed delivery pathway — please comment by email on whether our list is correct and complete, including a separate module for night-time.

dialogue.speaker: EXPERT_A
dialogue.text: Okay, let me just let me just translate donc du coup, [EXPERT_B], comme on a plus beaucoup de temps. En fait, elle propose qu'on continue enfin, que vous répondiez aux dernières questions par email qui sont plus factuelles. En fait, c'est moins. L'expérience, et c'est voilà, c'est. C'est plus sur les déclencheurs, finalement, des différents, des différentes situations, soit des refus ou des comportements. My… À voir si vous êtes d'accord avec la liste, s'il y en a trop, s'il y en a qui ont pas à être là s'il en manque. Je pourrais déjà le avoir pour qu'on ait une une cartographie. Finalement, de. De l'escalade, d'une situation. Qu'on comprenne bien comment. Comment elle intervient. Quoi? Okay, sorry, [INTERVIEWER], you can finish now.
dialogue.english_translation: Since we're short on time, she suggests you answer the last, more factual questions by email. They're less about experience and more about the triggers of the different situations — refusals or behaviours. See whether you agree with the list — whether there are too many, some that shouldn't be there, or some missing. So we have a map of how a situation escalates and how intervention comes in.

dialogue.speaker: INTERVIEWER
dialogue.text: The last two are about the escalation ladder — we're trying to make the escalation pathways (how care or intervention is triggered) systematic. Please comment and edit questions 11 and 12.

dialogue.speaker: EXPERT_A
dialogue.text: Donc du coup les les, la question 11 et 12: c'est ce qu'on appelle donc les l'escalade. Finalement, l'évolution de la situation. Et euh. En gros, il y a. Where Un espèce de de. D'une situation, comment elle elle évolue avec un comportement. Comment. On applique finalement l'approche Tcc, etc. En gros, c'est un peu le. Ouais, le déroulé de. On a un symptôme, comment on mesure comment on l'identifie, comment on. Prévoit une stratégie, comment on l'applique, comment on la mesure et après, est ce que.
dialogue.english_translation: Questions 11 and 12 are about escalation — how the situation evolves. How a situation evolves with a behaviour, how the CBT approach is applied — the sequence: a symptom appears, how we identify it, how we measure it… …plan a strategy, apply it, measure it, and then…

dialogue.speaker: EXPERT_B
dialogue.text: Ouais, j'avais noté oui, il manque. Par exemple, la fréquence est ce que c'est habituel ou pas.
dialogue.english_translation: Yes, I'd noted something missing — for example frequency: is it habitual or not?

dialogue.speaker: EXPERT_A
dialogue.text: Ouais, donc vous pourrez commenter là dessus, et ensuite, à la fin, c'est des choses qu'on a déjà évoqué au début de la réunion. Mais si vous avez d'autres commentaires à faire sur. L'exploitation en général. On en a parlé, mais si jamais il y a des choses qui vous reviennent en tête qui sont importantes. Finalement dans l'exploitation quotidienne des maisons.
dialogue.english_translation: You can comment on that; and at the end there are things we discussed at the start, but if you have other comments… …on operations in general, anything important in the daily running of the homes.

dialogue.speaker: EXPERT_B
dialogue.text: Oui, j'avais noté, par exemple, dans les stratégies par exemple, l'aménagement de l'environnement qui est hyper importante, la prévention du santé du corps aussi, qui est un point qui fait partie de notre méthodo et qui doit aussi transparaitre. Oui, Ben, quand faut-il ajouter d'autres alternatifs? Par exemple, la question huit. Il manque, il manque rien que oui, l'aménagement de l'environnement pour des routines, etc. Ça fait, ça peut servir de stratégie.
dialogue.english_translation: Yes, I'd noted, for example, under strategies: adapting the environment, which is extremely important; and preventive care of physical/bodily health, which is part of our methodology and should appear too. Yes — e.g., question eight, on when to add other alternatives. What's missing is adapting the environment for routines, etc. That can serve as a strategy.

dialogue.speaker: EXPERT_A
dialogue.text: Right. Okay. Okay, what [EXPERT_B] is adding is uh what he sees he will. He will work on this, and uh he will make some comments, but. Already he wants to say that. In his eyes. What's missing is a comment on the environment. Because in the [OPERATOR] method, the environment is very important. Um… in terms of stimulation, integration, socialization, et cetera. So there's nothing on an environment. And the other thing that's also interesting in our method is the [OPERATOR] method is body and mind in the sense that very often people with Alzheimer's when they have a behavior issue. You will say, oh, it's the disease speaking, but maybe he's got… a sore thumb, maybe he's got the wrong footwear, maybe he's hungry. So, before, you know, putting everything on the back of the disease, or blaming the disease for everything. First, clear everything that could be somatic, that could be related to the body, or the basic needs of the body. Um… And, you know, rule that out before saying it's because he's got Alzheimer's. And we find, he didn't say that, but I know that we found that 50% of the behavior issues are actually triggered by. Health or body related issues. So if you don't rule that out first, then you're missing the point most of the time. So have you checked? And it could be things that, it could be things that are not problems, but for example. Uh, that person is refusing to do what I tell him to do, but is that person wearing her hearing… hearing aids? Maybe that person is just not hearing me. So instead of saying, oh, he's refusing today, but no, it's just not hearing you. You know, read this for me. He's not wearing his glasses. How can I read this?

dialogue.speaker: INTERVIEWER
dialogue.text: Super helpful. I'll recap by email and would love his written input on questions 6–12, and any comments on the operations questions.

sessions.relevance: Medium. Two-layer record structure; why documentation detail matters; evidence-based inspections; frontline tool adoption; PC-only constraint.
sessions.excluded_content_categories: Illness small talk; revenue-capture and financial-statement analysis (revenue mix, costs, rent); upselling discussion; occupancy economics; investor/parent-group follow-ups.

knowledge_units.subtopic: Two layers in the record: coded actions vs observed narrative
knowledge_units.interviewer_question: (Interviewer presented analysis of a 25-resident record sample.)
knowledge_units.question_intent_why: Show what can be recovered from free text.
knowledge_units.expert_answer: Records contain (1) staff-coded responses (boxes clicked — their interpretation) and (2) free-text descriptions of what they saw. Reading the narrative against a structured clinical taxonomy and event-code library (refusal types, escalation ladder) produces a clearer care story. In this small sample, roughly a third of events were not coded and ~15% miscoded (indicative only).
knowledge_units.clinical_rationale_why: Raw observations are more reliable than staff's coded interpretation when reasoning frameworks are inconsistent.
key_points: Coded fields reflect interpretation; narratives reflect observation.
Structured re-reading can surface uncoded/miscoded events.
practice_rules: Base behavioural analysis on the narrative where coding is unreliable.
knowledge_units.cautions_or_corrections: Percentages are from a small, partial sample analysed by the interviewer's team; not validated.

knowledge_units.subtopic: Why detail matters in dementia documentation
knowledge_units.interviewer_question: (Interviewer rationale.)
knowledge_units.question_intent_why: Explains value of accurate behavioural documentation.
knowledge_units.expert_answer: Dementia care is behaviour-driven: every refusal, episode of distress or night-time wandering carries clinical meaning. Generic buckets in standard EHRs erase that meaning, making care invisible. In mid- to late-stage dementia every event is part of care; in a specialist setting the minimum bar is high.
knowledge_units.clinical_rationale_why: Precise documentation makes the specialised work visible and analysable.
key_points: Behavioural events have clinical meaning.
Generic coding loses it.

knowledge_units.subtopic: Quality inspections are evidence-based
knowledge_units.interviewer_question: (Discussion of value of better documentation.)
knowledge_units.question_intent_why: Links documentation to quality assessment.
knowledge_units.expert_answer: Quality control is proof-based; regular inspections by the national health quality authority grade homes, and the more evidence you can show of what you do, the better the assessment. Avoiding corrective actions after inspection also saves time.
knowledge_units.clinical_rationale_why: Documentation is how good practice becomes visible to regulators.
key_points: Inspections rely on documented evidence.
practice_rules: Document practice in a way that evidences the care approach.

knowledge_units.subtopic: Designing a frontline recording aid — and whether it will be used
knowledge_units.interviewer_question: (Interviewer showed concepts; expert asked whether another tool would make people record more.)
knowledge_units.question_intent_why: Test adoption assumptions.
knowledge_units.expert_answer: Interviewer design principles: don't make carers feel audited; recognise their work; show each resident's baseline so deviations get attention; guided reasoning (what happened → what was tried → outcome, e.g., 'settled'); reminders of non-drug approaches; immediate handover to the next shift. Expert: the real question is whether adding a tool leads people to fill in more — that must be tested; frontline staff have no incentive tied to documentation.
knowledge_units.clinical_rationale_why: Adoption depends on reducing burden and perceived usefulness, not on organisational benefit.
key_points: Baseline-deviation cues; guided reasoning; non-drug reminders; handover.
Uptake must be tested; incentives are weak.
practice_rules: Pilot any recording aid with frontline staff before scaling.

knowledge_units.subtopic: Keep specialist dementia populations dedicated
knowledge_units.interviewer_question: (Discussion of admitting residents without dementia.)
knowledge_units.question_intent_why: Clinical principle behind specialist units.
knowledge_units.expert_answer: The expert's principle: you don't mix the specialist dementia population with people without dementia — the setting is dedicated, like a treatment designed for a specific condition. (He noted that admitting less-impaired residents had nonetheless raised occupancy during a downturn.)
knowledge_units.clinical_rationale_why: Specialist environments, routines and staffing are designed around dementia-specific needs.
key_points: Dedicated dementia units should not be mixed with non-dementia residents.

knowledge_units.subtopic: Practicalities of engaging frontline staff
knowledge_units.interviewer_question: Could we show interviewees the tool?
knowledge_units.question_intent_why: Plan engagement.
knowledge_units.expert_answer: Only if you want their opinion — explaining the whole project takes too long and staff can't be kept off the floor. Frontline staff do not have smartphones; they work from PCs, so prototypes should look like the real PC-based environment.
knowledge_units.clinical_rationale_why: Respect care time; design for the actual hardware.
key_points: Keep sessions focused; don't over-explain.
Design for PCs (no smartphones on the floor).
practice_rules: Prototype on the hardware staff actually use.

dialogue.speaker: INTERVIEWER
dialogue.text: Illustration from a 25-patient sample of EHR records. The records contain two kinds of content: (1) staff-administered coded responses (the boxes/buttons clicked) and (2) a free-text description of the event. We ran our own logic over the raw descriptions using a clinical taxonomy (cascading from agreed principles on cognition, dementia and CBT) and an event-code library that categorizes refusal types and defines an escalation ladder. The output is a structured view of each care episode (the 'care story'), rather than the raw EHR view.

dialogue.speaker: INTERVIEWER
dialogue.text: This yields a clear clinical delivery flow, built from public research and expert input — not yet incorporating the operator's own method. In this small, limited sample, about a third of events were not coded at all and ~15% were miscoded (indicative only, ±5–10%; access was partial).

dialogue.speaker: INTERVIEWER
dialogue.text: Context matters because dementia care is very behaviour-driven. Every refusal, episode of distress or night-time wandering carries clinical meaning; a standard EHR loses most of that when events get dumped into generic buckets, so the care isn't visible. In a specialist dementia setting the minimum bar is already very high, and accurate documentation shows the extra work done.

dialogue.speaker: EXPERT_A
dialogue.text: Yeah. And and there's not only revenue. There's also quality control. Quality control is proof based. And now we have, you know, regular inspections. I don't know how often they come. Um… It's fairly recent. It's only been a few years. And the more evidence you can show, the better your grade will be. And that is not something that is directly translating into revenue. but not having to correct any any shortfall that they may have witnessed as part of the inspection. is effectively impacting positively your bottom line. Because there's that much time you don't have to spend on it. So what they call HES is the Health High Authority that is not supervising the quality of their homes. If if you can provide a lot more evidence of what you do. It really helps you in the assessment.

dialogue.speaker: INTERVIEWER
dialogue.text: The existing EHR captures two things: what staff did (their own interpretation/coding) and what staff saw (raw description of the event, without their reasoning). The raw description is valuable because it can be re-read against a structured reference framework.

dialogue.speaker: INTERVIEWER
dialogue.text: A frontline-facing feature idea: the tool should not make care aides feel audited but help them be more productive and feel recognized (e.g., positive feedback when they record); show each resident's baseline so anything outside it gets closer attention; offer a guided click-through of reasoning (what happened → what was tried → how it went, e.g., 'settled'); remind them of non-drug approaches in case training is forgotten under pressure; and pass the note to the next shift immediately.

dialogue.speaker: EXPERT_A
dialogue.text: But then what? But would this data be then populated into the EHR? Okay.

dialogue.speaker: INTERVIEWER
dialogue.text: Yes, it would plug into the EHR as an extension. Nobody performs well when micromanaged or treated as if they don't know their job; the aim is to make a tired care aide's job easier at 3 a.m. and make them feel part of something.

dialogue.speaker: INTERVIEWER
dialogue.text: Even if a human goes into the EHR today, much of it is not recorded — it may be empty.

dialogue.speaker: EXPERT_A
dialogue.text: Yeah, the question is… Is the real question is. adding another tool. Will adding another tool help people feel out more?

dialogue.speaker: INTERVIEWER
dialogue.text: Well, yes, if it makes the frontline people really engage and makes their life better and help them to do their job faster. They will. Otherwise, no, right? But also… But also the most important thing is that they also don't understand if they're not doing that job, it's costing the enterprise money.

dialogue.speaker: EXPERT_A
dialogue.text: Yeah, but that they don't care.

dialogue.speaker: INTERVIEWER
dialogue.text: No one… No, exactly. Because to them, you know, it's not, it's not, it's not, you know, they don't get any incentive. from making the enterprise money. They don't get a bonus for doing a better job. Same as the nursing homes. You don't get a bonus for doing a really better job than other people. So why bother? Just try not to cause any trouble.

dialogue.speaker: INTERVIEWER
dialogue.text: For residents with mid- to late-stage dementia, context is what's required: in a general nursing home 'the resident drank the orange juice' means little, but in dementia care every event is part of the care/therapy.

dialogue.speaker: EXPERT_A
dialogue.text: I agree with you. And that was something I was convinced of. For… forever. But very recently, our homes have been, you know, like every nursing home has been experiencing lower occupancy rates.

dialogue.speaker: EXPERT_A
dialogue.text: And what the parent group did… …to boost occupancy was to start admitting people without dementia, or without severe dementia. To my great surprise, that did boost occupancy — I'd always thought people with dementia would fill the homes. Maybe it's temporary, but it's a fact.

dialogue.speaker: INTERVIEWER
dialogue.text: Well, yeah. Yeah, but it's —. Yeah, it's a product. It's a better product. It's a much better product than the standard product. Who doesn't like this level of care?

dialogue.speaker: EXPERT_A
dialogue.text: No, but no, but it's not. You don't mix our population with non-demented people. They…

dialogue.speaker: INTERVIEWER
dialogue.text: Yes, yeah, but from the business standpoint, from the consumer standpoint, um, it's almost like it's a better product that can be subscribed to, so, yeah.

dialogue.speaker: EXPERT_A
dialogue.text: It's not, it's not, it's a dedicated, it's like, as if saying, oh, this drug works for this disease, you don't have that disease, but you can still get the drug, you'll feel better. Well, no, I don't have that.

dialogue.speaker: INTERVIEWER
dialogue.text: Well, they don't care about feeling better because they're not sick, right?

dialogue.speaker: EXPERT_A
dialogue.text: No, but they they won't. No, they won't see it that way. They'll just go. Okay, there's 1 around the corner. It looks nice. I'll go there. Has nothing to do with the quality of care that's delivered there.

dialogue.speaker: EXPERT_A
dialogue.text: It's too complicated for them. At this stage. I think. It would take too much. It would take too much time explaining, and I'd rather you focus on the interview and get what you want out of it rather than waste time, not waste time, but you know, spend time on explaining the whole project to them. It'll take forever. and you can't keep them off the field for too long, so rather use that time rather use that time really to get the info that you need.

dialogue.speaker: INTERVIEWER
dialogue.text: Mm-hmm. Oh, right, right, right. Oh! Yes, yes, yes, yes. But I thought it's, like, at least make the, uh, feature of the, you know, the end of the day, the recording application more intuitive. Um, I can show them that.

dialogue.speaker: EXPERT_A
dialogue.text: Well, if you want their opinion on it, then yes. But if it's just to show them as a reward for their time, don't bother. Bear in mind, because it looks very much smartphone-based, your app, from the screen I've seen. Bear in mind that they do not have smartphones. They only work from, they only work from a PC. Okay. Yeah, just to let you know, because I think it would be better, and I've been trying to convince them that to move to smartphones for 5 years now. But they won't budge on it. But so yeah, if you want to make it look as if it's the real work environment, don't make it look like it's from a phone.

dialogue.speaker: INTERVIEWER
dialogue.text: Mm-hmm. Yeah, on the PC. Yeah, yeah. Okay. Sure. Sure. I'll make we'll make those changes. Yeah. Sounds good. Awesome.

glossary.term: CBT-informed dementia care (TCC in French transcripts)
glossary.definition: Non-pharmacological care approach applying cognitive-behavioural principles to people with dementia: adapted environment, cognitive stimulation, structured strategies for behaviours. Experts stress it is not a 'treatment' and does not cure.

glossary.term: Personalised care plan (PCP) / individual cognitive care plan
glossary.definition: Individualised plan built from pre-admission information (life history, neuropsychological profile, abilities) and initial assessment; sets objectives that are reviewed. Agreed in a collegial multidisciplinary meeting; recorded by the psychologist.
Structured review ~1 month after admission assessing integration, orientation, socialisation, eating/weight, sleep and symptoms; usually leads to adjusting the initial plan.
Shift-to-shift information exchange, written in the care software and discussed in daily meetings; the psychologist attends to explain behaviours.
Resident declining a care task or activity. Must be qualified by domain, manner/intensity, frequency/recurrence and likely cause (care-delivery style, internal state, environment).
Behaviour of walking about; distinct from refusal; resource-intensive for homes.
Attempting to leave the home; per the clinical lead, not a refusal and not quite a behavioural disorder; common in newcomers; signals poor integration.
Loss of motivation/engagement; flagged by the clinical lead as an important, often unaddressed target and an entry point to further decline.
Method principle: repeated daily pleasurable experiences to stabilise mood and self-esteem; any antidepressant reduction is gradual and medical.
Checking pain, discomfort, basic needs and sensory aids (hearing aids, glasses) before attributing behaviour to dementia.
Mini-Mental State Examination — standardised cognitive screening test; consistently recorded in the homes discussed.
Neuropsychiatric Inventory — standardised scale of behavioural/psychological symptoms in dementia (mentioned as 'NPI, behaviour problems').
Country-specific scale of care dependency; used at facility level and linked to funding; not comparable across countries.
Employed physician (one per home, sometimes part-time) who coordinates residents' treating doctors, organises care provision and hygiene, and advises on treatments/behaviours; does not treat.
Senior nurse responsible for the nursing team; delivers flash trainings with the psychologist and coordinating physician.
Bulk of hands-on staff; main authors of daily records; no portable devices in the homes discussed.
Psychologists are not doctors and do not prescribe; psychiatrists are doctors who prescribe. The method relies mainly on psychologists.
Psychologist specialised in neuropsychology; in this dataset, the method's clinical lead.
Dedicated space within the nursing home where residents spend the day in structured activities and return to their rooms afterwards.
Room equipped for multisensory stimulation; observed at an overseas site applying the method.
Structured group activity (e.g., music) following a technical guide aimed at multi-area brain stimulation; form may vary.
Sequence: symptom appears → identify → measure → plan strategy → apply → re-measure; consider habituality/frequency.
Team review to find the root cause (physical, neuropsychological, or both) of a change or refusal; owner assigned by cause.
